newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada-U.S. bond spreads seen at new lows.
newsitem.headline: Canada-U.S. bond spreads seen at new lows.

text.p: The current spreads between Canadian and U.S. long-term bond yields will fall to record lows in coming months and may eventually disappear because of Canada's positive bond market fundamentals, analysts said.

"There's just nothing here that doesn't scream, 'Buy,'" said Randall Powley, a senior economist with Scotia Capital Markets. "We have substantially better numbers than in the U.S. and a substantially better outlook."
Canada-U.S. long bond spreads, which have fallen sharply this year, dropped to 11-year lows on Monday.

Analysts said the move was part of a growing recognition of Canada's superior bond market fundamentals. Those fundamentals, which include low inflation and reduced government borrowing, are seen narrowing spreads even further.

"We think prospects are still good for further narrowing. There's no doubt that yields at the 10-year maturity will go through those of the U.S.," said Anita Lauria, an economist with Salomon Brothers.
The yields on Canadian 10- and 30-year bonds on Monday narrowed to close at 25 and 63 basis points respectively above the yields of their U.S. counterparts.
The decline brought spreads to their lowest level since 1985 and marked a sharp decline from 10- and 30-year spreads of 152 and 165 basis points respectively at the beginning of the year.

Canadian bonds have historically offered higher yields than those in the United States, due to higher inflation, relatively high government borrowing and political uncertainty surrounding Quebec's secessionist movement.
But in the past three years, many of those factors have changed for the better.

The Canadian yield curve therefore began to trade through the U.S. curve at the three-month level earlier this year. Canadian bonds as far out the curve as five years are now trading with yields below those in the United States. Some analysts have forecast that the entire Canadian yield curve could soon trade below that of the United States.

"The shift in Canada's fiscal balances, both at the federal and provincial level, has opened up the door for Canada's yield curve to shake itself free of the U.S. yield curve," said Carl Weinberg, chief economist with High Frequency Economics.
A drop in government borrowing is the most cited reason for Canada's bond market outperformance relative to that of the United States.
Canada's budget deficit has shrunk drastically in the past three years, helped by sharp spending cuts by Canadian Finance Minister Paul Martin.

In fiscal 1993/94, the deficit rose to a record C$42 billion. But later today, Martin is expected to report he undershot his C$32.7 billion deficit target for fiscal 1995/96 ended March 31 by more than C$4.5 billion. The deficit is expected to fall even further in the next two years.
Deficit reduction has also occurred at the provincial level, with seven of Canada's ten provinces expected to balance their budgets this year and next.
Less borrowing by governments has contributed to another positive change in Canadian economic fundamentals -- a turnaround in Canada's balance of payments.
In August, Canada reported its first quarterly current account surplus in 12 years, meaning Canada was no longer reliant on foreigners to finance its deficits.
Canada's increased credibility on fiscal policy was matched with credible monetary policy, analysts said.
"There's no inflation risks (in Canada) compared to the U.S., where capacity is being strained and there is a risk of some inflation," said Salomon's Lauria.
Canada's inflation rate has been below the U.S. rate for several years. Canadian inflation was about 1.4 percent in August, versus a U.S. rate of about 2.9 percent in August.
With the market recognizing Canada's low inflation and improved fiscal situation, bonds are now being priced off of Canadian economic fundamentals rather than U.S. bond yields, analysts said.
With Canada's inflation rate showing no signs of accelerating, and economic growth in Canada relatively subdued, there is more room for Canadian long-term bonds to outperform U.S. Treasuries.

"It's difficult to imagine a situation over the next five years where Canada doesn't have significantly better fundamentals than the U.S.," said Scotia Capital Markets' Powley. "We've been doing all the right things. The restructuring in Canada has been painful and I think it's a situation of maximum pain, maximum gain here."
-- Reuters Toronto bureau (416) 941-8100
